summary: Describes a simplified method for extending the Link State PDU space beyond the 256 LSP limit in IS-IS. A router that needs to advertise more information can use additional system-ID-based fragments. It is intended as the preferred replacement for the method in RFC 3786.

eli5.summary: A router has a limited number of pages to describe itself. When it has more to say, this gives it a simple way to add more pages, so nothing important gets left out.

questions: how to increase is-is lsp space
what is the is-is 256 lsp limit
how do extended lsps work in is-is
what is the is-is alias id tlv
subtitle: A simpler way for an IS-IS router to advertise more than 256 LSPs by using extra system IDs.

tldr.problem: IS-IS limits a system to 256 LSPs per level, and newer features such as multi-topology and traffic engineering can exceed that capacity.
tldr.mechanism: The network administrator gives a router additional system-ids. The router originates extra LSP sets under them, with restrictions on content so that older routers still compute the same shortest path tree.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3786 as the preferred method and avoids the interoperability restrictions of that approach, though its value is limited unless all systems support it.

today: RFC 5311 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3786. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The 256 LSP Limit
sections.content:
The IS-IS specification limits the set of LSPs a system can originate at each level to 256, and sets a maximum LSP size (originatingLxLSPBufferSize) of 1492 bytes. That capacity has been enough in existing deployments, but new information such as multi-topology support, traffic engineering information and router capabilities could exceed it.

The problem first drew interest with traffic engineering extensions, which led to RFC 3786. That solution has restrictions needed to stay interoperable with systems that do not support it. This RFC lets a system go beyond 256 LSPs with no interoperability issues for such systems, and calls it a simpler and therefore preferred solution.
sections.eli5: A router can only write a fixed number of pages about itself. New features want more pages than that, so it needs a safe way to add some.

sections.title: Terms Used
sections.content:
The Originating System is the single physical IS. It originates LSPs on behalf of multiple virtual ISs. Its Normal system-id is the usual one. An Additional system-id is assigned by the administrator so that Extended LSPs can be generated, and it must be unique throughout the area (Level-1) or domain (Level-2).

An Original LSP uses the Normal system-id in its LSP ID, and an Extended LSP uses an Additional system-id. An LSP set is all LSPs of a given level with the same system ID and Pseudonode ID, so only the LSP number octet varies. The Virtual IS is the system identified by an Additional system-id and advertised as originating the Extended LSPs.
sections.eli5: The real router is like a person who gets a second name tag. Pages written under the second name still belong to the same person.

sections.title: Additional System IDs
sections.content:
An Originating System may be assigned additional system-ids to generate additional LSP sets. They follow the same rules as normal ones: unique within the Level-1 area, or within the domain at Level-2. The IS-IS Update Process treats Extended LSPs like normal LSPs for generation, flooding and purging. If the Extended LSP with LSP number zero and remaining lifetime above zero is missing for an additional system-id, none of the LSPs in that Extended LSP set are processed.

To tie the two together, the Original LSP set MUST include a neighbor to the Virtual IS for each Extended LSP set, with a metric of zero. This guarantees that the two-way connectivity check succeeds and that reaching the Virtual IS costs the same as reaching the Originating System. Where multi-topology is supported, an MT IS Neighbor advertisement is needed for every topology in the Extended LSP set.

Legacy routers simply see the Extended LSPs as information about a system reachable only via the Originating System. Nothing else is reachable via the Virtual ISs, so their SPF calculation stays consistent with that of extension-capable systems. That is why the two operating modes and the logical-LSP SPF handling from RFC 3786 are not needed.
sections.eli5: The router writes extra pages under its second name and tells everyone the second name is right next to it, at zero distance. Old routers just think there is a tiny dead-end neighbor.

sections.title: Restrictions on Extended LSPs
sections.content:
To avoid interoperability problems, Extended LSPs may carry only certain content. TLVs 3 (ES Neighbors), 4 (Part. DIS) and 5 (Prefix Neighbors) MUST NOT appear. An extension-capable IS ignores them, SHOULD report an error, and processes the other TLVs normally.

Leaf advertisements are allowed, for example TLVs 128, 130, 135, 235, 236 and 237. Including them requires advertising a neighbor between the Originating System and the Virtual IS. Neighbor reachability in an Extended LSP is limited to the Originating System, and that advertisement MUST use a non-zero metric and SHOULD use MaxLinkMetric-1.

LSP number zero of an Extended LSP set MUST include an Area Address TLV whose addresses are a subset of those in the normal LSP number zero at that level. The Overload (OL), Attached (ATT) and Partition Repair (P) bits MUST be 0 in all Extended LSPs. A set ATT bit could make legacy systems use the Virtual IS as a default exit point from the area.
sections.eli5: The extra pages may only hold harmless details, not anything that changes how routes are chosen. That way old routers cannot be tricked into sending traffic the wrong way.

sections.title: New TLVs: IS Alias ID and Neighbor Attributes
sections.content:
LSP number zero of an Extended LSP set MUST carry the new IS Alias ID TLV (type 24), which names the Normal system-id of the Originating System. Its value is a 6-octet Normal System-id, a 1-octet sub-TLV length and 0 to 248 octets of optional sub-TLVs. No sub-TLVs are defined here, and future ones MUST follow the format in RFC 5305.

Because TLVs 22 and 222 are barred from Extended LSPs except to advertise the neighbor to the Originating System, two more TLVs carry neighbor attribute information such as traffic engineering sub-TLVs: IS Neighbor Attribute (TLV 23, same format as TLV 22) and MT IS Neighbor Attribute (TLV 223, same format as TLV 222). They may appear in Original or Extended LSPs, but MUST NOT be used to infer a neighbor relationship that TLV 22 or 222 does not show in the Originating LSP set.

The IANA section registers TLVs 23, 24 and 223 as valid in LSPs only.
sections.eli5: The extra pages begin with a note saying 'I belong to this real router'. There are also extra forms for adding more details about a link than fit on the normal page.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
Several considerations limit the value of Extended LSPs unless all systems are extension-capable. Legacy systems cannot make much use of information carried in Extended LSPs, so implementations that add new TLVs which may go in Extended LSPs SHOULD also support this RFC.

If the Originating System sets the OL bit in a normal LSP, legacy systems see the Virtual ISs as unreachable, so extension-capable systems MUST do the same. This avoids routing loops when leaf information is in Extended LSPs.

When neighbor attribute data appears in both Original and Extended LSPs, non-conflicting data is additive. If it conflicts, the Original LSP wins, otherwise the Extended LSP with the lowest system-id is preferred. TLV 22 (or 222) information beats TLV 23 (or 223). Leaf information in Extended LSPs forces forwarding plane updates, so the RFC recommends keeping it in the normal LSP set when possible.
sections.eli5: The trick works best when every router knows about it. If the real router goes quiet, its twin must be treated as gone too, and when two pages disagree, the main page wins.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The RFC says it raises no new security issues for IS-IS. General IS-IS security considerations are in RFC 5304.
sections.eli5: Nothing new is risky here, and the existing security rules for IS-IS still apply.
